utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. We are here for another Status Conference in the case of Mr. Martic. Could you please, Madam Registrar, call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-11-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Shall we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. For the Prosecution, Mark McKeon, and I, Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff, trial attorneys, and with us is Ms. Lakshmie Walpita.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm getting the translation in French. It would be better to follow that in English. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour. I am Predrag Milovancevic, attorney-at-law, Defence counsel for the accused, Mr. Milan Martic, and my junior colleague and assistant, attorney Vuk Sekulic from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Sekulic. I agree. Thank you. Mr. Martic, please, do you understand what is being said here in a language you can completely understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Okay. You may sit down, please. Well, ladies and gentlemen, we have a few problems this time to be tackled with. First of all, since the OTP was already committed its pre-trial brief and even in due time, May the 7th, we had passed over to fix a moment for the presentation of the pre-trial brief by the Defence. So I suppose, Mr. Milovancevic, that you have already made -- taken your message through to be in due time when your pre-trial brief would be required. I should say that it would be more than three weeks later than the previous one, but I should like to hear what could you have to suggest? In principle, I would like to have your pre-trial brief ready for the first half of September, next September. So I take it into consideration that you have had some problems in getting some documents from the Croatian government and from other sources. Would you please tell me what is your stand on the facts, on those facts, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question, Your Honour, and I will reply as briefly as I can. The standpoint of the Defence with respect to its readiness to submit a definite version of its pre-trial brief in accordance with Rule 65 ter is defined by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the Statute. The response of the Defence in connection with the deadlines that we have to speak about is connected with three essential points which I will set out very briefly by Your Honour's leave. The first of these points has to do with the application of Rule 21 of the Statute, which provides for minimum guarantees of the accused's right to defence with respect to time and the means necessary for the preparation of a defence. For the reasons that I have already mentioned at the Status Conference in January and which I will only briefly reiterate now, the Registry is persisting in keeping Mr. Martic's case at the second level. Mr. Martic is accused of participation in a joint criminal enterprise, and the Prosecution, in its indictment, states that he had positions of leadership over a five-year period, and the Prosecution in the indictment alleges that his activity took place on the territory of two countries of -- or, rather, two former socialist republics of the former Yugoslavia, that is Croatian, Bosnia and Herzegovina. And bearing in mind the allegation in the indictment that Mr. Martic's activity was connected with the activities of a significant number of other participants in the joint criminal enterprise, bearing in mind also Mr. Milosevic and the extent of his case is well known to the Defence, and also bearing in mind that the indictment against Mr. Martic accuses him of joint activity with at least 11 other co-accused who have been indicted before this Tribunal, bearing all this in mind the Defence fails to see the reasoning for the Registry that this case in its complexity corresponds to the second level. A direct consequence of this, Your Honours is that the Defence has received information from the Registry that by February, or that is as of February, the members of the team, some members of the team no longer have the means to carry on their work, and the others no longer have these means as of March. For the further work of this Defence team in preparing the response to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief as well as further investigations which are or which were carried out up to now by Mr. Martic's Defence team, the first issue to be resolved is the issue of the level of this case. In view of the fact that the Defence team has done its very best and has exhausted all means addressing the Registry, on the 29th of April, the Defence team submitted a urgent motion to the Trial Chamber asking that this issue of the level of the case be resolved. A case of this extent and this complexity in the nature of things belongs to the third level. That is how it appears to the Defence, Your Honour. That is the first issue. And the Defence hopes that the Trial Chamber will understand Mr. Martic's need for his Defence team to continue its work based on the normal expectation that the Trial Chamber will permit the Defence team to continue its work by ordering the Registry to classify this case as a third-level case. This whole situation is linked to a circumstance that is well known to this Chamber and to you yourself, Your Honour, and that is that the Defence has agreed to do a large amount of work in processing unselected material instead of the Prosecution; that the Defence has spent ten months doing this; and, that by exerting enormous efforts in ten months they have done a job which, according to the Prosecution, would have taken two or three years for the Prosecution to do. In this case, the Defence cannot even consider the proposition that it has wasted its energy and the means at its disposal that it has acted irrationally or that it has in any way failed in its obligation to conduct its work in the best possible manner. Therefore, the Defence team expects that with respect to the issue of category, it will obtain the support of the Trial Chamber. And that was the first issue I wished to raise, Your Honour. The second issue is linked to the time needed by the Defence to give a definite rely to the Prosecution pre-trial brief, and this has to do with the fact that the Defence received the entire brief on the 14th of May of this year. The brief has 47 pages of text and three annexes. Annex A dealing with issues which are not in dispute, this is three pages long. Annex B, which contains a lot of witnesses to be called by the Prosecution, and this annex has a total of 122 pages. And Annex C containing a list of exhibits that the Prosecution intends to present during its case. This annex is 219 pages long. So that actually, Your Honour, there are 391 pages altogether, not counting the appendix with the list of sources attached to the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, and this has 13 pages. Another important fact should be stressed, Your Honour. The Prosecution disclosed to us a large number of CDs along with its pre-trial brief. These CDs contain documents that the Prosecution wishes to present, so that the final pre-trial brief, in accordance with Rule 65 ter (E), contains 1.640 pages of material which are completely new under Rule 66(A)(ii). In this list of material, it says 12.335 pages of material in the shape of written documents that the Prosecution wishes to tender during its case. So the total amount is 13.900 pages of written text that has not yet been disclosed to the Defence, which the Defence has not yet read and which the Defence is duty-bound to familiarise itself to be able to respond in accordance with Rule 65 ter (F). This Rule provides that the Defence has to respond to all of this material in the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution. It must be borne in mind that the complete pre-trial brief of the Prosecution has also additional 13 video CDs. The Defence must also view this material, and simply to read this newly disclosed material according to the criteria recognised by the Registry, a total of 1.300 hours is required if they say that 60 documents can be analysed per hour. The next point that should help us to define the time needed by the Defence for -- to prepare its pre-trial brief is linked to disclosure by the Croatian government. In January we raised this issue at the Status Conference, and we had a meeting on this topic with the senior legal officer and the Prosecution this year. The Defence accepted Your Honour's advice, and after a brief pause, after a brief time to allow the newly elected Croatian government to start its work, the Defence addressed a fourth letter to the Croatian government which received in the second half of February this year, indicating that the government is duty-bound under the Tribunal's rules to supply materials to the sides before this Trial Chamber and reminded them again of all materials sought prior to that date and asking for some additional material. Your Honour, we have received no reply to date. The work of the Defence in a case of this category and with that kind of indictment, and the indictment is for participation in a joint criminal enterprise, the Defence is unable to prepare for this unless it receives the material required from the Croatian government. The third and last issue I wish to raise, which affects the time when the Defence will be ready to fulfil its obligation is connected to disclosure under Rule 68 by the Prosecution. This disclosure has been carried out so far according to the criteria that the OTP itself set up in connection with Mr. Milosevic a year ago. Your Honour, we told you that the Prosecution disclosed to us a enormous amount of material according to these criteria. This is over 4.000 pages, but no selection of these materials was carried out. The Defence undertook to go through this material, and we have done so as Your Honour has been informed, and this disclosure has been continuous and is still ongoing. In order to understand the position of the Defence, it is very important to understand the following, Your Honour: After making a selection of the material disclosed under Rule 68, and after the Defence established what there is in this material and what is of importance to us, the Defence has continuously, at the same rate as it went through this unselected material, sent requests to the Croatian government for delivery of those materials not supplied by the Prosecution under Rule 68 and which were suggested by the Prosecution itself in its letter of May last year. Your Honour, the Defence, on four occasions, in August of last year, the 20th of August, to be precise, the 8th of October, the 25th of December, and now in late February, asked for a certain number of very important documents from the Croatian government important for the Defence, but we have not received any reply. However, from the contacts we have had in the meantime with a view to -- on the part of the Prosecution to assist us in obtaining this material - I'm referring to a meeting, a 65 ter meeting in April of this year - the Defence established that the Prosecution in fact does possess some of these materials which are of crucial importance to us but that it cannot disclose those materials to us either because it feels that these materials are not relevant to us or because they consider that some of these materials were obtained in a confidential way or because some investigations having to do with these materials are ongoing and they feel that disclosing this material would influence and pre-judge the course of these investigations. The final reason presented by the Prosecution for the non-disclosure of these documents which they evidently have is a written statement that this is a vast amount of materials scattered throughout the collections of the Prosecution and. According to the Prosecution's letter, this would be a monumental task for the Prosecution to carry out. None of these reasons stated by the Prosecution in its letter of the 27th of April of this year, Your Honours, is a reason recognised by the Rules for the Prosecution to fail to comply with Rule 68. If some of these materials are more important for the work of the Prosecution in other cases, the Prosecution can request measures from the Trial Chamber in order to comply with the Rules. In any case, there is another point I wish to make. In January, the Defence told the Prosecution that all the materials supporting the case against Generals Gotovina, Markac, and Cermak. Markac and Cermak were accused of a joint criminal enterprise on the Croatian side in order to forcibly expel the Serb population from the territory of the Krajina as was carried out by perpetrating the crimes listed in the indictment by the expulsion of several of hundreds of thousands of Serbs. All the supporting materials for this indictment in the nature of things, in view of the fact that they refer to the territory of Croatia and the areas in which according to the Prosecution Mr. Martic was active, and in view of the fact that they refer to the period of time in which Martic was active, all these materials, in the view of the Defence, are exculpatory materials under Rule 68, without a doubt. The Prosecution, in paragraph 11 of the indictment against Generals Gotovina, Markac, and Cermak, states that this is a joint criminal enterprise in which the former president of the Republic of Croatia Franjo Tudjman participated, and the top leadership of Croatia. And not only does it speak of the Operation Storm which took part from the 4th of August to, according to the Prosecution, mid-November, but in paragraph 50, 51, and 52 of the same indictment, Your Honours, they say that the Croatian leadership planned this before 1992, since before 1992, that the UNPAs and the pink zones connected to the Vance plan should be taken by them through armed operations, which was done. And in paragraph 52 of this indictment the Prosecution states that this was done by operations Miljevacki Plateau in 1992, Maslenica in 1993, in January, Medacki Dzep, in September 1993 Operation Flash in May 1995, which is directly linked to our indictment, and Operation Storm. Not only that, the Prosecution raised -- issued another indictment against Jadranko Prlic and Alis [as interpreted], Croats from Bosnia who are charged with acting with the complete Croatian leadership including Franjo Tudjman; Minister of Defence, Mr. Susak; Chief of Staff, Janko Bobetko; and other unnamed individuals with the objective of creating a greater Croatia. This activity took place allegedly from at least the 18th of November, 1991, until April, 1994, or even later. Despite its greatest efforts to understand the position of the Prosecution that this material is not relevant to the Defence under Rule 68 and with all due respect for the position of my learned friends from the Prosecution, the Defence finds that what happened in the territory of Croatia and Bosnia at the same time, in the same period with the only difference that participants involved were not the same, but the activities took place in the same period that is relevant for Mr. Martic, and still they don't recognise that it could be exculpatory material under 68(A). But at the same time that it could be material which could help the Defence rebut the basic stand of the Prosecution that it is a joint criminal enterprise. For this reason, the Defence believes that disclosure of this material cannot be avoided by the Prosecution and that in not disclosing it the Prosecution violated its obligations. Since we pointed out this problem as far back as several months ago, the Defence believes it is now upon the Trial Chamber to issue an order to the Prosecution to disclose all the relevant material which is relevant under the very criteria determined by the Prosecution, and especially the supporting material for these two indictments against Jadranko Prlic and the Croatian generals, Gotovina, Markac and Cermak, because this material is not any longer unselected and unsearched. This Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is the supporting material resulting from the investigations already conducted by the Prosecution. And let me add one more thing at this point. The Prosecution notified through the media that it conducted investigations against Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Izetbegovic. The relevant criteria are included in the list of possible material to be disclosed to this Defence suggested by the Prosecution themselves. However, we did not receive any of it. Therefore, I kindly ask of you, Your Honour, to acknowledge my apology for taking so much time in this introduction, but the only reason for taking so long is that the problems the Defence is facing now are so serious. The response of the Defence to the final pre-trial brief of the Prosecution should be filed at the moment when nine years after issuing the indictment against Mr. Martic for the shelling of Zagreb and one year after the amended indictment against Mr. Martic for participating in a joint criminal enterprise, the Prosecution is now in May filing its final pre-trial brief under Rule 65 ter (E). If at this moment the Defence is still lacking the material that I referred to, the question arises how and in what time frame we can receive this material and only then will we be able to inform the Trial Chamber about the time within which we can file our pre-trial brief in a realistic manner. If the Prosecution took so long to prepare their case, it is certain that with the resources it has, the Defence is already in a difficult position, and without this material it is unable to do the -- its job because of the complexity of the situation it finds itself in. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. I think you have put to me a lot, to me and to the Prosecution also, a lot of problems altogether. Let's arrange your words, if I may say so, and start by one thing, and then we'll follow the other. Let's for the moment -- for the time being, let's have aside the problem of the delaying of the case. That is something I will tell you about later on. But now the problem, the substantial problem we have now is to know when you will be ready with your pre-trial brief. You had mentioned many aspects that I would like also to hear the Prosecutor about, but be aware, and I have to insist on that, that my task is to try to make an expeditious disposition of this case. Although it would never be unfair, it has to be very expeditious in the solution. And let's say that the expeditiousness in many ways is at the same time a part of the fairness for the accused who deserves to be judged in a shorter -- in the shortest time possible. I will hear, before making a solution, about what the Prosecutor believes about that, but let me tell you that you haven't taken advantage of the possibilities of asking the -- from the Prosecutor a lot of documents that maybe have not been provided to you by the Croatian authorities, but perhaps you don't need to go there since you are being offered by the Prosecutor to get some of these documents. Let me remind you also that the provision made in the Rule 67(C) has previously disappeared, because this Rule that provided for the reciprocal disclosure in case you asked for some disclosure of some material will oblige you to discover also these other materials to the Prosecution. This is not any more or anything that can be operated like that because this provision has already been repealed. So don't hesitate now to ask the Prosecution for whatever you need in the way of documents you may require. And don't try to insist, if it is not necessary, absolutely necessary, to get those documents from the Croatian government. So that's something I say to begin with. I will stand myself on these matters after I have heard the Prosecutor about them, and so thus only to begin. Please may I ask the Prosecutor to know which are their beliefs and their opinions about what has been suggested about the time that has been required for introducing his pre-trial brief by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, in answer to your question, I just want to refer to what is actually expected by the Defence. The Defence, at this point in time, is supposed to provide a pre-trial brief in which it only in general terms explains the nature of its defence, the matters that it will take issue with from the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution and give also reason why it takes issue. It is not expected at this point in time from the Defence to know all the details of all the evidence as possible that will be provided during trial. There is no need for them to go into any details of this evidence. It's not necessary to discuss all the details of the events that happened. All what is needed is to get an idea of the general nature of the Defence, and that, I think, can be done until, as you proposed, the first half of September. And the course the Defence needs to have the means and needs to have a big enough Defence team to deal with the documents that were now provided and at least can read it and study it and then make their position, make up their position. This is the first thing I wanted to stress. Secondly, the Defence has said, "We can't, we can't possibly make our Defence brief before we not get all these additional materials dealing with the actions of the opposing forces," that is the Croatian -- the Croatian forces and the Bosnian Croat forces. The Prosecution has in discussions and also in writing explained that that is not relevant. What is relevant is to see what actually are the charges, what is this accused charged with, and not what the Croats did. That's a different case. That's the case against Mr. Gotovina. That's the case against the other gentlemen that Defence counsel mentioned. There is a profound error when the Defence feels that the fact that the Croatian forces committed crimes elsewhere and at different times, that this would be exculpatory for the actions he did. He is charged with ethnic cleansing in certain territories at certain times, but he comes up telling us, "I can only defend myself when I have the material that relates to actions of the Croat forces in 1993, 1995," totally unrelated to the charges here in the indictment we are dealing with. And this is what we try to stress. We have looked at the materials of these so-called flip-side cases, and we have provided limited Rule 68 materials because we do not believe, and it's not our position that whatever these other perpetrators did during Operation Storm, during operation flash, exculpates this accused. This is why we do not provide such materials. And we do not need it according to the Rules. We do not need to search for irrelevant materials. But my colleague Mr. McKeon may add -- want to add to this. Another point -- what else was stressed? No, these are actually the two points what I want to make. That is what is now at the moment whatever requested they can perform in the time limit given by the Judges, of course when they have the Defence team and the means to pay for the Defence team. That's a different issue, and it's on the agenda, and I will only speak about this when we come to this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Would you like to intervene also now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: I'd like to speak on the point when we get to it of the production of the materials from the Croatian government, but I think I can hold my remarks until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: I believe this is the correct moment for doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: The only other point that I'd like to add to what Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff has said is that the Defence has now available to it the electronic disclosure suite of documents which has a large volume of materials on it; it will by the end of the year have an even larger volume. This material is searchable through web access that is available to the Defence counsel. In addition, I understand that it is possible for all documents that have been disclosed by the Prosecution to the Defence to also be put on this disclosure suite so that they can then search through all documents that we have already given them and do their own searches to find the documents that they believe may have some relevance. So there will -- there's now the ability to find many of these documents themselves through that electronic disclosure suite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: I would like also to know from you - you may sit down, please - whoever of you can answer me, if I have understood well, the counsel for the Defence suggests that you haven't complied with the disclosure that was necessary for this other party with the material. Is that correct? You still have not disclosed whatever is necessary for the Defence, or what is your answer to this claim of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to our records, we have actually complied with our obligations. We have made Rule 68 searches, and what came up so far in these searches was disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But there is this disagreement between the parties that the Defence feels that whatever the Croats did in what -- at whatever location, at whatever time is relevant for them, which would mean a huge amount of documentation which we say is not relevant. And the fact that the Prosecution alleges a joint criminal enterprise on the Croat side in relation to certain time periods, that does not anything for this accused. That's an issue for the other case, not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With regard to what my learned friend Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff has just said concerning the necessary content of the Defence trial brief, of course I agree. There is nothing controversial about this. The Rule 65 ter (F) clearly defines what the Defence is supposed to include in the pre-trial brief. What is important, however, is that the Defence and the Prosecution do not agree about one important matter, and the Prosecution views this as a fundamental error of the Defence, namely that the Defence proceeds from the position that whatever the Croatian or any other side did in terms of crimes is exculpatory for Mr. Martic. This is not a position that we have ever taken, Your Honour. Our position is something different. The Prosecution in their very pre-trial brief state that the incidents, and I'm quoting: "The incidents charged Skabrnja, Lipovaca, Bacin, and many other places enumerated in the indictment. All these places are not all for which Mr. Martic is charged. They're only the most typical, only some of the incidents. The Prosecution does not charge Mr. Martic for the direct perpetration of any crime. The responsibility, the liability of Mr. Martic is defined by the indictment in a joint criminal enterprise, and in order to understand, establish, and verify whether this joint criminal enterprise existed, we have to establish what actually happened on the ground in the territory of Croatia and in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the years of war. It is not that we are saying that these indictments against Markac, Cermak, Jadranko Prlic and others from Herceg-Bosna concerning 1995 are relevant for our case, but the matter is that on the same territory for which Mr. Martic is charged, large parts of Croatia and large parts of Bosnia at the same time, which is relevant for Mr. Martic, there was a different activity with totally opposite objectives. I am not talking about the crimes from other indictments. I'm not saying that it is a Croatian joint criminal enterprise, and I don't agree, as the Defence counsel for Mr. Martic, with the position of the Prosecution. I will try to show the opposite, the opposite of their case, which is that there was a joint criminal enterprise involving Mr. Martic. I'm not going into the merits of the case, but I have to explain what the essence is. If we are dealing with the same events at the same time in one territory, we must have all the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, let me tell you something from the very beginning. It is that we are not just now making the adjudication of the case. That will come later in a real moment of hearing the case. All these points could be, of course, completely irrelevant. Don't forget that now you are only supposed to answer and to say with which issues you take issue that have been mentioned and brought about by the Prosecution. So that is the point now, to make this pre-trial brief of you. That would help us to have a pre-trial meeting that will make -- start the case. That is the moment in which you will need all that. And I would say that the aspect that you insist so much about the participation of your defendant in a joint criminal enterprise is some point that has not to be proven. It is just for the Prosecution to prove. If it has been proven beyond a possibly doubt by the Prosecution, you don't have to exert a lot of effort in this way. So let's come back again to try to point out aspects that has to be discussed so as to try to expedite the solution of this case. First of all, you are trying to insist on asking to the -- for the -- from the Croatian authorities a lot of documents. That couldn't be useful if you allow me to tell that unless you before tried to get them from other sources, and one source which has been offered to you repeatedly is that the Office of the Prosecution can provide you with some of these documents you seem to be looking for from the Croatian authorities, the Croatian government. So that is one point. So then try to revise aspects that are absolutely for your defence, for defence of your client, and limit yourself to those and not try to cover yourself with a lot of work to be done because you are getting too many documents, many of which are not relevant to the position you have and couldn't really be taken into consideration by the Chamber whenever they have to decide. So that's something important. Secondly, it seems to me that the disclosure by the Prosecution has been completed, and in case some new documents appear, you will be given notice, information about them. So don't make things so complicated and try to ease the situation, because that could be helpful for you and for the work of this Chamber. Another point I would like to mention, perhaps you haven't brought it about before, is the agreement on facts. You have made an answer on some of the facts that has been submitted to you by the Prosecution, and I find that some of them, why are you not agreeing with that? That's, for example, would you -- this is included on number 10 on the proposal of agreements made to you already one year ago in May the 5th, 2003, by the Prosecution. This point, for instance, just picking up some of these points, on 21st December, 1990, Serbs in Knin announced the creation of the Serbian autonomous district of Krajina and declared their independence for Croatia. Why didn't you agree with that? That's a point that wouldn't be so difficult or so compromising for your client to be agreed on. So that's just an example of what can be done so as to reduce your work, the burden of your task, which unless you resort to this sort of procedures, you are going to, of course, find it absolutely unbearable. Please try to limit yourself to what is really interesting, important. I don't want to limit your freedom to add in the way you believe you have to, but try to be more concise and that would allow you to give you the possibility of presenting to us the pre-trial brief in the four months. You say that you haven't been given notice of the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief until May the 14th. Well, let's make it four months exactly unless the -- and let's have your pre-trial brief no later than September the 15th. So I believe if you resort to some of these means and these ways of operating, you will reduce very much your task and you will be able to have this at this moment. Another point which has been mentioned by you is the Defence motion about the upgrading of the case. We are getting information about that, and the most I can say just now is that we are going to have pretty soon an answer, I mean the Chamber is going to give you an answer about that. So most probably, most probably I would say that you're going to get your motion accepted. It doesn't seem, even if it looks for you, and I'm very glad in many ways. You find it a complicated case, but not so much so as to be upgraded to level three. But let's give time for you to get the answer for that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So I would insist again in the points I had mentioned to you before so as to shorten the possibilities for you to have your pre-trial brief at the date I mentioned and I'm establishing. You see that the Prosecutor has made this in a far briefer period of time, so please try to abide by this according which the Rules I had already had mentioned to you. In the sense that I -- my task is to make you to meet, both parties, the Prosecutor and the counsel for the Defence, to brief -- to shorten the time, the delay, that would be required for completion of your task. And besides that, I will always be reachable to you if you have an extra problem, but I believe if you are accepting, which I am pointing out like the delay for presenting your pre-trial brief, the four months, you will have time enough to prepare it. I wonder if you would like to point out some other problem at this very moment before we keep proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, only according to the agenda do I see that we are actually asked to respond to the Defence motion in relation to the upgrading of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's not up -- it's up to the Registrar and the Trial Chamber to classify the level, but what can be said, and we concur here with the Defence, it is a complex case covering events in Croatia and Bosnia over an extended period of time, but of course it's not the whole war, not everything what happened in the war, only a very limited territory that we are concerned here with. But nevertheless, it is a complex case with complicated legal issues of command responsibility and culpability for actions of other members of the joint criminal enterprise, and there are a lot of complicated factual issues. Therefore, I think it can be said that it is a complicated case that needs a lot of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: You mean that you are mentioning that it could be upgraded to level three?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's not up to us to say what makes something level 3. What is the big distinction between level 2 and level 3. That's for the Registrar to have an opinion on. All I can say is that it is a complicated case that is actually definitely within the higher ranks of the cases here in the Tribunal. It's not compare -- comparable to the Milosevic case but definitely to cases like generals and other local leaders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your help. Is there anything else, Mr. Milovancevic, you would like to raise now, another question that you feel that could be needed to be solved at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood your suggestions, Your Honour, quite accurately regarding my pre-trial position, and I understand that I should not go into the merits. I bear that in mind all the time, and I always will. I only wanted to say one more thing to avoid a false impression regarding the course of our cooperation in agreeing on points, on various facts. You chose, Your Honour, number 10 out of all the points, and you asked me why we find it hard to agree with the propositions of the Prosecution. I will reply that we gave the Prosecution a response which was based on the Statute and the legal enactment adopted at the time. Unlike the Prosecution, I will not go into commenting the contents of that legal enactment, but we quoted verbatim the decision envisaging Serb autonomy within the framework of Croatia. To my mind, in my reading, that is something different from proclaiming independence. What it actually means will be discussed at trial. However, we approached the process of negotiation in good faith, and we found it possible to agree on certain points. We made suggestions regarding the Operation Storm and the Vance plan, and the Prosecution found it impossible to agree. However, we found it nowadays, the same text that we proposed, we find nowadays in the Croatian indictments. I only want Your Honour to bear in mind that all the factual and legal issues are viewed by us as extremely important because they define the existence or non-existence of things the Prosecution claims, and we are very delicate in our approach. Every time we try to quote verbatim the documents referred to by the Prosecution, but the Prosecution takes it upon themselves to interpret them. Unlike them, we always use direct quotations. The Prosecution did not accept many of our responses and even erased them as points that could be agreed. I had to say this because you -- otherwise you might get a false impression about our cooperativeness. Our job and our intention is to help the accused and to cooperate fully, with that in mind, with our learned friends from the Prosecution. Let me add one more thing. I am thankful to my colleague from the Prosecution for saying what I understood as support to the request of the Defence for upgrading the case. Indeed the issues are very complex, and we can see that from the fact that on the date of the previous Status Conference in January we received 21.000 pages of new material, and by now we have received another 14.000 pages. If we view this in the light of the 14 September deadline, we have to bear in mind these indicators of the complexity of the case. I am just trying to explain the problems that we are facing in our attempts to assist the accused in the way we consider the best for him. And let me say one more thing before I conclude. The Prosecution mentioned that as far as the other indictments are concerned, the supporting material is not relevant for us, and they did not even wish to search it. However, I have to disagree. For the preparation of our defence, this material is crucial because it has a qualifying importance for the acts of the accused in this case. We are not trying to stand in the way of an expeditious trial. With the resources it receives eventually and with the material available to us at this stage, the Defence with make every effort to perform its duty. However, with all due respect to your efforts to help both parties, I must reiterate that the issue of disclosure in this case is of vital importance and will determine our ability to prepare our defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you again, Mr. Milovancevic. I am sure, and I am very glad to have heard you to say that, you are proceeding in the best good faith. That is very important. You may consider that also from the part of the Prosecution you don't -- you cannot expect a trick to be played on you and your client. So I am very happy that you maintain this idea, and I completely trust you in this way, because I have to, and besides, I am sure of your goodwill in this case. So please try to abide by the time limits we are going to -- I mean, we are setting to you, and don't hesitate in coming to us whenever it would be necessary, when you feel it is necessary for you in extra help. As far as I am concerned, I am at your disposal for that, and that is my task also. Well, if nothing else has to be mentioned now on other issues, I'm going to ask Mr. Martic how does he feel, how -- do you have to present us with some problem in relation with your -- I am speaking to you, Mr. Martic. Are you having any problems with your health, mental or physical, and would you like to raise them here to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As for the conditions in the Detention Unit, I have no objections. By your leave, I would like to say something very briefly about my defence. I would like to say that I am extremely satisfied with the work of my Defence counsel, but I appeal to you as a neutral party to exert your influence to ensure that there is equality of arms between my Defence and the Prosecution. It seems to me that this is not really correct behaviour on the part of the Prosecution. At one point, it seemed to me that they were Defence counsel for Croatia. I ask Your Honour to make it possible for my counsel to defend me in the best possible way. My legal advisor on the team was not allowed to visit me in the defence unit the last time he was here, and this was repeated again. I'm sure that the legal advisor can also be useful. This is just a banal example. However, as far as I am concerned, I can hardly wait for the trial. I feel that I am innocent, but please make it possible for me to put up a good defence. Only you can do that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: You may be completely sure that the neutrality of this Chamber and that it will take care that the position of your defence is at the same level of capacities than that of the Prosecutor. I have an extra question to ask you. You have problems meeting with your -- your counsel or you have all the conveniences and the moments and the time required for preparing well your defence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just told you, Your Honour, a specific example. We asked for more time to work here -- to work together. This means a lot to us. But he was not granted a sufficient number of hours here, and the legal advisor was not allowed to come in. I don't see where the problem is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: You mean he hasn't time enough to confer with you and to -- I mean, to speak up about the case as much as you feel is required? I mean, you are not given in the Detention Unit time enough to confer with your counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is probably that there are so many of us in the Detention Unit and we are unable to get rooms to work in. So our time is limited. We would have a lot to time but the time is limited because, simply, there are no facilities, no rooms for us to work in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Well, you could ask for extra time, perhaps, in the Detention Unit or you haven't required this extra time? Exactly what would you like to be done in --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it seems that the matter is getting complicated now. My Defence counsel asked for more time to confer with me. He was unable to obtain this because there were many visits. The Detention Unit was crowded, and no rooms were available for us to work in. It's not complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: Even if the Detention Unit, as you say, is crowded, I suppose in the occasions and the places for conferring lawyers -- I mean, counsel -- counsels and accused persons, you have to ask for the required time, and I have to be sure that you get it. So I will try to see about that and find out what is, because you need and you deserve to have all the time required for that. Of course, I am speaking in the normal behaviour nothing, not really would be in our views, and I grant on you for that. Well, I think we have to have another Status Conference in a matter of one -- not less than 120 days, which is approximately the time at which I am expecting to get the pre-trial - you may sit down, please - the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: And if nothing else is to be brought about here, I think we are going to adjourn the case. Oh, no. Go ahead, Mr. Milovancevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour, but in connection with what the accused just said, my client Mr. Martic, with respect to visiting hours in the Detention Unit, there really are technical problems because there are many inmates in the Detention Unit, and there are insufficient -- there's insufficient room on the premises. But this, however, is not a complaint. I wish to say something else in view of the volume of brief which the Prosecution has sent to the Defence, which is 390-something pages, and we have two, three, four hours at the most to confer with our defendee, I ask that this material be translated as soon as possible into the language of the accused so that he can familiarise himself fully with the case against him and the evidence that is to be presented against him. Objectively, a long time would be needed for me as his counsel to translate this material for him which he cannot understand, and I would not like to bring him into a position as his counsel for him -- his understanding of these documents to depend on my translation. There are professional services which should do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MARTIN-CANIVELL
utterances.text: We will try to see about that, and thank you for telling me about this problem. So the session is adjourned.
